name: Char Kway Teow
description: Flat rice noodles stir-fried over very high heat with garlic, soy sauce, chilli paste, prawns, blood cockles, Chinese sausage, chives and bean sprouts, traditionally in pork fat. Created as cheap fuel for Chinese labourers, it is a hawker favourite in Malaysia; in Penang it is often served on a piece of banana leaf.
how_to_eat: Eat hot from the wok, ideally with its smoky 'wok hei' still fresh.
how_to_order: Order a plate at a hawker stall; say if you want it without cockles or extra spicy.

name: Penang Asam Laksa
description: Thick rice noodles in a sour fish broth made with mackerel and tamarind (asam), topped with cucumber, onion, mint, pineapple and a spoon of sweet shrimp paste (hae ko). It is Penang's signature laksa.
how_to_eat: Stir the shrimp paste into the broth before eating.
how_to_order: Ask for 'asam laksa' at Penang hawker centres and coffee shops.

name: Penang Hokkien Mee
description: Egg and rice noodles in a rich prawn-and-pork broth, topped with prawns, sliced pork, egg, kangkung and fried shallots with sambal. In Penang 'Hokkien mee' means this prawn soup, unlike the dark fried version of Kuala Lumpur.
how_to_order: Ask for 'Hokkien mee' or 'prawn mee' at Penang hawker stalls, usually a breakfast dish.

name: Nasi Kandar
description: Steamed rice served with a choice of curries, fried chicken, fish, squid and vegetables, with several curry gravies poured over ('banjir'). It was created by Tamil Muslim vendors in Penang who carried rice and curry on a shoulder pole (kandar).
how_to_eat: Ask for mixed gravies over the rice and eat with your right hand or a spoon.
how_to_order: Point at the dishes you want at a nasi kandar shop; ask for 'kuah campur' for mixed curry gravy.

name: Penang Rojak
description: A fruit and vegetable salad tossed in a dressing of shrimp paste, sugar, chilli and lime, topped with crushed peanuts. The Penang version adds water apple, guava, squid fritters and honey, with a very thick, almost toffee-like dressing.
how_to_order: Buy it from rojak stalls at hawker centres and beaches.

name: Cendol
description: Shaved ice with green pandan rice-flour jelly, coconut milk and palm sugar syrup (gula Melaka), often with red beans. It became a hawker staple in Penang and is listed as a heritage food by Malaysia's Department of National Heritage.
how_to_eat: Stir everything together and eat quickly before the ice melts.
how_to_order: Buy a bowl from cendol stalls; red beans are a common add-on.

name: Chicken Rice Balls
description: Hainanese chicken rice where the seasoned rice is shaped into golf ball-sized balls, served with chopped poached chicken and chilli sauce. Serving the rice in balls is the custom in Malacca and Muar.
how_to_eat: Eat the rice balls with the chicken and dip in chilli sauce.
how_to_order: Order at chicken rice ball shops in Malacca.

name: Ayam Pongteh
description: A Peranakan (Nyonya) stew of chicken cooked with taucu (salted fermented soybeans) and gula Melaka, giving a salty-sweet flavour. Pongteh is also made with pork, as a Nyonya take on Chinese braised pork belly.
how_to_eat: Eat with steamed rice.
how_to_order: Look for it at Nyonya restaurants.

name: Nyonya Laksa
description: Noodles in a rich coconut-milk curry broth (laksa lemak) with prawns, cockles, tofu puffs and hard-boiled egg, with sambal belacan. It is a classic of Malacca's Nyonya (Peranakan) cuisine.
how_to_order: Ask for 'laksa Nyonya' at Peranakan cafes.

name: Devil's Curry
description: A very spicy Kristang (Malacca Portuguese-Eurasian) curry flavoured with candlenuts, galangal, mustard seed and vinegar. Its name comes from the Kristang 'debal' (leftover), as it was made from Christmas meal leftovers a day or two after Christmas; it is the most popular Kristang dish.
how_to_eat: Eat with rice or bread.
how_to_order: Ask for 'kari debal' at Kristang (Portuguese-Eurasian) eateries in Malacca.

name: Satay Celup
description: Skewers of seafood, meat, tofu and vegetables dipped and cooked in a pot of boiling spicy peanut sauce at the table. It is a Malacca speciality.
how_to_eat: Dip skewers into the shared pot of peanut sauce; you pay by the number of sticks.
how_to_order: Go to a satay celup restaurant and pick skewers from the fridge.

name: Onde-onde
description: Small glutinous rice balls coloured with pandan, filled with liquid palm sugar and rolled in grated coconut. They are a classic Malay and Nyonya kuih.
how_to_eat: Pop a whole ball in your mouth so the palm sugar bursts inside.
how_to_order: Buy from kuih stalls and Nyonya bakeries.

name: Nasi Lemak
description: Rice cooked in coconut milk and pandan, served with spicy sambal, fried anchovies, peanuts, cucumber and boiled egg, often with fried chicken or rendang. It is widely considered Malaysia's national dish.
how_to_eat: Mix a little sambal into each mouthful.
how_to_order: Buy a banana-leaf-wrapped 'nasi lemak bungkus' in the morning or a plated version at mamak shops.

name: Roti Canai
description: An unleavened, flaky flatbread of Indian origin whose name probably comes from the Malay 'canai', to roll dough thinly. It is served with dal or curry at mamak (Indian Muslim) stalls, and in 2024 Malaysia had it listed by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage together with nasi lemak and teh tarik.
how_to_eat: Tear pieces and dip them in the dhal or curry.
how_to_order: Order 'roti canai' at a mamak shop; 'roti telur' adds egg.

name: Bak Kut Teh
description: Pork ribs simmered in a herbal broth with garlic, star anise, cinnamon and other Chinese herbs. Klang in Selangor claims to be its birthplace.
how_to_eat: Eat with rice and fried dough sticks dipped in the soup, with Chinese tea.
how_to_order: Order at bak kut teh shops in Klang, usually for breakfast.

name: Satay Kajang
description: Grilled skewers of marinated meat served with peanut sauce and rice cakes. Kajang-style satay, said to have been started there in 1917, is known for its larger chunks of meat and peanut sauce served with a side of fried chilli paste.
how_to_eat: Dip the skewers and rice cakes in the peanut sauce.
how_to_order: Order skewers by the stick at satay restaurants in Kajang.

name: Hokkien Mee (KL)
description: Thick yellow noodles braised in thick dark soy sauce with pork, squid, fish cake and cabbage, topped with crispy fried pork lard. Also called Hokkien char mee, it was developed in Kuala Lumpur, reputedly by hawker Ong Kim Lian on Petaling Street in 1927.
how_to_order: Order 'Hokkien mee' at Chinese hawker stalls in Kuala Lumpur.

name: Ampang Yong Tau Foo
description: Tofu and vegetables such as chilli, bitter gourd and aubergine stuffed with fish paste, served in broth or dry with sauces. Ampang, on the edge of Kuala Lumpur, is famous for it.
how_to_order: Pick your pieces and choose soup or dry style.

name: Teh Tarik
description: Black tea with condensed milk, 'pulled' by pouring it between two vessels from a height to give a frothy top. It is Malaysia's national drink.
how_to_order: Order 'teh tarik' at any mamak shop; 'kurang manis' means less sweet.

name: Ipoh White Coffee
description: Coffee beans roasted with palm-oil margarine, brewed and served with condensed milk. It originated in Ipoh, which Lonely Planet named one of the top three coffee towns.
how_to_order: Order 'white coffee' hot or iced at Ipoh old town kopitiams.

name: Bean Sprouts Chicken
description: Poached chicken served with a plate of crunchy local bean sprouts dressed with soy sauce and sesame oil. Ipoh's bean sprouts are credited to the hard water from the limestone hills of the Kinta Valley.
how_to_eat: Eat with rice or flat rice noodle soup.
how_to_order: Order chicken and a plate of bean sprouts at Ipoh's chicken shops.

name: Ipoh Kai Si Hor Fun
description: Smooth flat rice noodles in a clear chicken and prawn broth, topped with shredded chicken and prawns. It is one of Ipoh's best-known noodle dishes.
how_to_order: Order at Ipoh coffee shops, usually for breakfast or lunch.

name: Ipoh Salted Chicken
description: A whole chicken wrapped in grease paper with salt and Chinese herbs and baked for several hours, which keeps the meat tender. It is a traditional Hakka dish that Ipoh is known for.
how_to_eat: Tear the meat apart by hand.
how_to_order: Buy a whole wrapped chicken from salted chicken shops in Ipoh.

name: Tau Fu Fa
description: A velvety pudding of very soft silken tofu, traditionally flavoured with brown sugar syrup. It is one of Ipoh's well-known desserts.
how_to_order: Buy a bowl at tau fu fa shops in Ipoh.

name: Nasi Kerabu
description: Rice coloured blue with butterfly-pea flowers, served with fresh herbs and greens, salted egg, fish crackers, stuffed chillies (solok lada) and fried chicken or fish. It is a traditional dish of Kelantan and Terengganu.
how_to_eat: Mix the herbs, coconut and sauce into the rice.
how_to_order: Look for it at Kelantanese stalls and markets.

name: Nasi Dagang
description: Rice steamed with coconut milk and fenugreek, served with a tuna (tongkol) curry and pickles. It is a typical breakfast in Terengganu and Kelantan.
how_to_order: Buy it in the morning from Terengganu breakfast stalls.

name: Keropok Lekor
description: Chewy, sausage-shaped fish crackers made from ground fish and sago flour, seasoned with salt and sugar and deep-fried. It was created by Terengganu fishermen as a way to preserve fish during the monsoon season.
how_to_eat: Dip in chilli sauce.
how_to_order: Buy freshly fried keropok lekor from roadside stalls.

name: Laksam
description: Thick rolled flat rice noodles in a rich, slightly sweet white gravy of minced fish and coconut milk, served with ulam (raw salad) and shredded herbs. It is a Kelantanese favourite, also found in other northern and east coast states.
how_to_order: Ask for 'laksam' at Kelantanese breakfast stalls.

name: Ayam Percik
description: Marinated chicken grilled and basted with a spiced coconut milk gravy, also called ayam golek in some states. It is a well-known Kelantanese dish.
how_to_eat: Eat with rice.
how_to_order: Look for it at Malay food stalls in Kelantan.

name: Akok
description: A caramel-flavoured cake made from eggs, coconut milk, flour and brown sugar, cooked in a brass mould over charcoal. It is a traditional Kelantanese kuih.
how_to_order: Buy from kuih stalls in Kelantan markets.

name: Laksa Johor
description: Spaghetti served in a thick gravy of grilled wolf herring (ikan parang), concentrated coconut milk, onion and spices, topped with raw vegetables and herbs. Its use of spaghetti sets it apart from other laksa.
how_to_order: Look for it at Johor Malay eateries, especially on festive days.

name: Mee Rebus
description: Egg noodles in a thick, spicy and aromatic gravy thickened with cooked, mashed tuber vegetables, probably of Javanese origin. It is one of Johor's notable dishes.
how_to_eat: Squeeze the lime over before eating.
how_to_order: Order at Malay hawker stalls.

name: Otak-otak
description: Fish paste mixed with chilli, garlic, shallots, turmeric, lemongrass and coconut milk, wrapped in leaves and grilled over charcoal. Muar in Johor is renowned for its version, wrapped in attap (nipa palm) leaves.
how_to_eat: Unwrap the leaf and eat the fish cake inside.
how_to_order: Buy by the piece at otak-otak stalls in Muar.

name: Asam Pedas
description: A sour and spicy fish stew, its sourness coming from tamarind or dried asam keping, simmered with chillies and spices. In southern Johor the gravy is thicker and often seasoned with black pepper, while Muar, Batu Pahat and Kluang favour a thinner version without pepper.
how_to_eat: Eat it with steamed rice.
how_to_order: Ask for 'asam pedas ikan' (fish) or 'asam pedas ayam' (chicken) at Malay eateries.

name: Mee Bandung Muar
description: Yellow noodles and egg in a thick gravy of dried shrimp, onion, spices, shrimp paste and chillies, later topped with prawns, meat, fish cakes and vegetables. The dish originated in Muar, Johor, and 'bandung' means 'mixture' in Malay.
how_to_order: Ask for 'mee bandung' at Malay stalls in Muar.

name: Sarawak Laksa
description: Rice vermicelli in a broth of sambal belacan, coconut milk, tamarind, garlic, galangal and lemongrass, topped with shrimp, chicken strips, omelette and bean sprouts. Also called Kuching laksa, it was called the 'Breakfast of the Gods' by Anthony Bourdain.
how_to_eat: Squeeze the calamansi lime into the broth.
how_to_order: Ask for 'laksa Sarawak' at Kuching coffee shops in the morning.

name: Kolo Mee
description: Dry noodles tossed in pork fat and shallots, topped with char siu pork slices and fried shallots. It traces its history to Kuching's Chinese community and was gazetted as a Malaysian heritage food in 2024.
how_to_order: Order at Kuching coffee shops; 'red' kolo mee adds char siu sauce.

name: Manok Pansoh
description: Chicken cooked inside bamboo with lemongrass, ginger and tapioca leaves over an open fire. It is a traditional Iban dish.
how_to_eat: Eat with rice.
how_to_order: Look for it at Dayak restaurants and longhouse visits.

name: Umai
description: Raw sliced fish or other seafood cured in calamansi lime juice and tossed with ground peanuts, sliced onions and chillies. It is a traditional Melanau dish of Sarawak, eaten with toasted sago pearls.

name: Kek Lapis Sarawak
description: A colourful, intricately patterned layered cake baked layer by layer from butter, eggs and flavourings. It is a Sarawak speciality, served at festivals.
how_to_order: Buy slices or whole cakes from kek lapis shops in Kuching.

name: Hinava
description: Raw fish (often mackerel) cured in lime juice with chilli, ginger, shallots and grated bambangan seed. It is a signature Kadazan-Dusun dish.
how_to_order: Look for it at Kadazan-Dusun restaurants.

name: Tuaran Mee
description: Springy handmade egg noodles fried until crispy, briefly boiled, then stir-fried with egg, choy sum and slices of char siu. It comes from the town of Tuaran in Sabah, where it was created in 1952.
how_to_order: Order at coffee shops around Kota Kinabalu and Tuaran.

name: Ngiu Chap
description: A beef noodle soup with poached beef slices, meatballs, brisket, tendon, liver and other offal. It was brought by Hainanese migrants to Jesselton (now Kota Kinabalu) around the 1930s and is an iconic Sabahan dish.
how_to_order: Order at beef noodle shops in Kota Kinabalu; choose soup or dry noodles.

name: Lihing
description: A fermented glutinous rice wine of the Kadazan-Dusun people, most associated with Penampang. It is served at the Kaamatan harvest festival.

name: Pinasakan
description: A Kadazan-Dusun dish of fish, usually mackerel scad, simmered with salt, turmeric and sour takob akob fruit or bambangan until the liquid reduces to a concentrated gravy. It began as a way for interior Dusun communities to keep fish through a day's work in the fields, and is cooked without oil.
how_to_eat: Eat it with white rice, linopot or ambuyat.

name: Sinalau Bakas
description: Wild boar meat marinated with salt, garlic, ginger, lemongrass and turmeric, then smoked for several hours over a slow wood fire. Sinalau is the traditional smoked meat of the Kadazan, Dusun, Murut and Rungus peoples of Sabah.
how_to_eat: It is commonly eaten with beer.
how_to_order: Buy it at roadside stalls on the Tamparuli to Kundasang road or at markets in interior districts such as Ranau, Tambunan and Keningau.
